nodes.name: Biceps brachii
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: The most superficial muscle of the front compartment of the upper arm (teachmeanatomy.arm_muscles); its belly forms the front of the arm. Unchanged from the shipped record.
nodes.databaseMuscleNote: Shipped value; exists in the canonical list (shared/capabilityRank.ts).
nodes.statusReason: Both function claims on the node are reviewed: forearm:biceps.function (shipped) and upper_arm:upper_arm.biceps.function.
nodes.location: Front of the upper arm, at the surface: its two heads start on the shoulder blade, join, and cross the elbow to the radius.
nodes.whatItDoes: Bends your elbow and turns your palm up; with the elbow bent it is the strongest palm-up muscle. It also crosses the front of the shoulder, where it gives only weak help raising the arm forward.
nodes.shapeNote: May contribute most of the front contour of the upper arm, between the shoulder and the elbow crease, since it is the surface muscle there. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: Its two heads are one muscle here: they end in one tendon and share their actions at the elbow and forearm.
Its help raising the arm forward is weak, and studies disagree on whether it is active at all in shoulder movement, so that is not counted as a shoulder action here.
Some people have an extra head; it usually causes no symptoms.
membershipCaveatsForForearm: It is an upper-arm muscle and does not add forearm size.
Shown only as another muscle that curls and palm-up turning load; not a forearm target.
nodes.neutralTextNote: Replaces the shipped shapeNote 'Shapes the front of the upper arm. It is an upper-arm muscle and does not add forearm size.' and the shipped caveat 'Shown only as another muscle that curls and palm-up turning load; not a forearm target.', whose region-relative words move to the forearm's membership of this node (§1.3).

nodes.name: Brachialis
nodes.outcropSupported: Yes: Kenhub's video page says it has superficial portions at its lateral border and distally (kenhub.brachialis_video), which is the §7.2 'brachialis outcrop beside the distal biceps on Front-surface'.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Mostly hidden under the biceps, with its outer edge and lower end near the surface (kenhub.brachialis_video; A51; teachmeanatomy.brachialis). Unchanged from the shipped record.
nodes.databaseMuscleNote: Shipped value; exists in the canonical list.
nodes.statusReason: Its only function claim, forearm:brachialis.function, is reviewed.
nodes.location: Front of the lower half of the upper arm, under the biceps, crossing the elbow to the ulna.
nodes.whatItDoes: Bends your elbow, whichever way the palm faces. It does not turn the forearm.
nodes.shapeNote: Mostly covered by the biceps, so most of it has little or no contour of its own. Its outer edge near the elbow lies close to the surface and may add to the outer side of the lower upper arm, beside the biceps. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: It bends the elbow whatever the grip, so curls with the palm down or the thumb up load it too.
membershipCaveatsForForearm: It is not a forearm muscle.
Shown only as another muscle that curls load; not a forearm target.
nodes.neutralTextNote: Replaces the shipped shapeNote 'Mostly covered by the biceps; may show at the sides of the lower upper arm. It is not a forearm muscle.' and caveat 'Shown only as another muscle that curls load; not a forearm target.'; 'at the sides' becomes 'outer edge', the only edge the sources confirmed.

nodes.name: Triceps brachii
nodes.layer: — (§1.2; parent, neither drawn nor selectable; the TypeScript value follows the platform lane, the forearm's groups use 'mixed')
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Two heads at the surface and one mostly under them (radiopaedia.triceps_brachii; kenhub.triceps_brachii_video); the forearm marks its mixed-layer groups 'partial'.
nodes.databaseMuscleNote: The canonical list holds the three heads, not the whole muscle.
nodes.statusReason: Its function claim, upper_arm:upper_arm.triceps.function, is reviewed.
nodes.location: Back of the upper arm, from the shoulder blade and the upper-arm bone to the point of the elbow.
nodes.whatItDoes: Straightens your elbow. Its long head also helps move the arm down and back at the shoulder.
nodes.shapeNote: Together its three heads make up most of the back of the upper arm. Which head shapes which part of that outline cannot be read exactly from the surface. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: A muscle with three heads, not a target itself: work is counted for the heads inside it.

nodes.name: Triceps, long head
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: At the surface and easy to feel (kenhub.triceps_brachii_video; anatomyzone.triceps_lateral_head), but no source names its own outline as a visible landmark apart from the lateral head; the forearm marks such surface muscles 'partial'.
nodes.databaseMuscleNote: Exists in the canonical list (shared/capabilityRank.ts); the database lane confirms.
nodes.location: Back of the upper arm, at the surface, from the shoulder blade just below the shoulder joint down to the common tendon at the point of the elbow.
nodes.whatItDoes: Straightens your elbow with the other two heads. It is the only head that crosses the shoulder, where it helps move the arm down and back and toward the body, and helps hold the top of the upper-arm bone in its socket.
nodes.shapeNote: May contribute to the back-of-arm contour from below the shoulder toward the elbow, as one of the two surface heads. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: Its actions at the shoulder are small next to its work at the elbow.
Short-term studies find its share of the work changes with arm position; that is activity, not growth, and it is not used to weight credit.

nodes.name: Triceps, lateral head
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: At the surface on the back and outer side (radiopaedia.triceps_brachii; kenhub.triceps_brachii_video), outline merging with the long head; 'partial' as for the long head.
nodes.databaseMuscleNote: Exists in the canonical list; the database lane confirms.
nodes.location: Back of the upper arm on the outer side, at the surface, from the upper half of the upper-arm bone to the common tendon at the point of the elbow.
nodes.whatItDoes: Straightens your elbow. It does not cross the shoulder.
nodes.shapeNote: May contribute to the outer part of the back-of-arm contour, as one of the two surface heads. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: It shares every action with the medial head, so their work is counted together and not split between them.

nodes.name: Triceps, medial head
nodes.outcropSupported: Supported on balance, with a disagreement: Radiopaedia says it lies largely deep to the lateral head, Madsen 2006 found its muscle reaching further toward the elbow than the other two heads, and DocCheck Flexikon says only its lower part shows from outside; Kenhub's video says it cannot be felt. Not a deviation; the claim and caveat say references differ.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Mostly covered; at most a small lower part near the elbow reaches the surface, and references differ on that (see outcropSupported).
nodes.databaseMuscleNote: Exists in the canonical list; the database lane confirms.
nodes.location: Back of the upper arm, deep layer, on the lower half of the upper-arm bone under the long and lateral heads; its lower part reaches closer to the elbow than theirs.
nodes.whatItDoes: Straightens your elbow, and draws the back of the elbow joint's capsule out of the way as it straightens. It does not cross the shoulder.
nodes.shapeNote: Mostly covered by the long and lateral heads, so it has little or no contour of its own; its lowest part, just above the elbow, may show a little. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: It shares every action with the lateral head, so their work is counted together and not split between them.
References differ on whether any of it can be felt through the skin.

nodes.name: Coracobrachialis
nodes.layerSupported: Supported in part: it lies behind the pectoralis major near the shoulder and on the inner side of the biceps and brachialis (elsevier.coracobrachialis; kenhub.coracobrachialis), so a front view with the arm by the side shows little of it; Kenhub says it is easiest to feel in the armpit, where it forms the outer edge with the humerus. Not a contradiction of 'deep' for a drawing of the arm at rest; no deviation proposed.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Slender and covered near the shoulder; felt in the armpit, not seen as a contour of its own.
nodes.databaseMuscleNote: No coracobrachialis row among the canonical names in shared/capabilityRank.ts.
nodes.location: Inner side of the upper part of the upper arm, from the front of the shoulder blade to about halfway down the upper-arm bone; behind the chest muscle near the shoulder and on the inner side of the biceps below it.
nodes.whatItDoes: Raises your arm forward at the shoulder and helps draw it in toward your body.
nodes.shapeNote: Slender and mostly hidden near the shoulder, so it has little or no contour of its own. It can be felt in the armpit. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: Shown beside the upper-arm muscles because of where it sits; upper-arm specialization does not target it.

claims.statement: Whether the way the palm faces changes how hard the biceps works in a curl is not settled. In a surface-EMG study of ten bodybuilders, the biceps was more active with the palm up than with the palm down or the thumb up while lifting, with no difference reported while lowering; in a surface-EMG study of 16 people making slow single elbow bends, its activity did not change between the three positions. Neither study measured growth.

claims.statement: Studies disagree on whether the biceps works in shoulder movement at all. With the elbow braced straight, a wire-electrode study of ten shoulders recorded no activity in its long head during shoulder movement; a surface-EMG study of 13 healthy people found low long-head activity that rose when the arm was raised forward or out to the side. A scoping review of the long head concluded that its part in raising the arm is minimal in healthy shoulders. None of these studies measured growth.

claims.statement: Two small training studies compared elbow extensions done with one arm overhead and the other down by the side. In 21 adults over 12 weeks, measured muscle volume rose more in the overhead arm, in the long head and also in the lateral and medial heads together; in nine novice women over six weeks, triceps thickness and strength rose similarly in both arms. These are group results from short studies, not a forecast for any one person, and they are not used to weight credit.

sources.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Triceps Muscle (Bordoni)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (introduction and parts of Structure and Function): the primary function of the triceps is elbow extension; the three heads join in one tendon on the olecranon; the long head arises from the infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula and, because it attaches there, has a small action on the glenohumeral joint, and with the arm adducted helps hold the head of the humerus in the glenoid cavity; the medial head does not attach to the scapula and has no action on the glenohumeral joint. PubMed 30725681. One result gave the editor as Bruno Bordoni and the update date as 28 Aug 2023; the full author list was not shown.

sources.title: Kenhub: biceps brachii muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026: function line lists flexion and supination of the forearm at the elbow joint and a weak flexor of the arm at the glenohumeral joint; the scapular origin lets it act on both the shoulder and the elbow. The French and German pages returned no function text.

sources.title: Kenhub: triceps brachii muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026: long, medial and lateral heads from the scapula and humerus inserting via a common tendon on the ulna; long head from the infraglenoid tubercle, lateral head from the posterior humerus above the radial groove, medial head below it; the main function is extension of the forearm at the elbow; the long head contributes to extension and adduction of the arm at the shoulder joint.

sources.title: Kenhub video: triceps brachii muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (video description only): the long and lateral heads are easily palpated because they lie more superficially; the medial head cannot be felt because it is tucked beneath them. The video itself was not seen.

sources.title: Kenhub video: brachialis muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (video page preview only): the brachialis is mostly hidden under the biceps brachii and hard to palpate from the surface, with superficial portions at its lateral border and distally. Nothing was found about its medial edge reaching the surface.

sources.title: Kenhub: coracobrachialis muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026: a long, slender muscle of the anterior compartment of the arm from the coracoid process to the shaft of the humerus; medial to the biceps brachii and brachialis; with the humerus forms the lateral border of the axilla, where it is easiest to palpate; main actions are flexion and adduction of the arm at the shoulder; musculocutaneous nerve. A stabilising role for the humeral head appeared only in a Kenhub video transcript.

sources.title: Elsevier Complete Anatomy, Quick Facts: biceps brachii
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026: origin on the supraglenoid tubercle and the apex of the coracoid process; inserts on the radial tuberosity and antebrachial fascia; supinates the forearm and flexes it at the elbow, most effectively when supinated. No shoulder action is listed.

sources.title: Elsevier Complete Anatomy, Quick Facts: lateral head of triceps brachii
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026: origin on the posterior humerus above the radial groove and the lateral intermuscular septum; inserts on the olecranon, where the three heads converge on one tendon; extends the forearm at the elbow; radial nerve (root level given as C6, which another source disputes).

sources.title: Elsevier Complete Anatomy, Quick Facts: medial head of triceps brachii
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026: origin on the posterior humerus below the radial groove; inserts on the olecranon and adjacent antebrachial fascia; extends the forearm at the elbow; some fibres attach to the elbow joint capsule and are regarded by some authors as a separate muscle (articularis cubiti). The search summary said its own citation markers were partly garbled; the facts matched the IMAIOS entry.

sources.title: Elsevier Complete Anatomy, Quick Facts: coracobrachialis
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026: origin at the apex of the coracoid process; inserts on the middle third of the medial humerus; adducts and flexes the arm at the glenohumeral joint; musculocutaneous nerve, which pierces it; posterior to pectoralis major and medial to brachialis and biceps brachii.

sources.title: IMAIOS e-Anatomy: long head of triceps brachii
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (imaios.cn mirror): action line lists elbow extension and shoulder extension and adduction; with the arm adducted the long head helps hold the humeral head in the glenoid cavity; the only head that crosses the shoulder. IMAIOS's veterinary entries describe the shoulder differently; only the human entry is cited.

sources.title: Radiopaedia: triceps brachii muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026: a three-headed muscle in the posterior compartment of the arm; elbow extension is the main action, the long head assisting shoulder extension and helping steady the shoulder (described in abduction); lateral head from the posterior and lateral humerus above the radial groove, extending to the lateral intermuscular septum; medial head from the lower posterior humerus below the groove and largely deep to the lateral head.

sources.title: Loyola University Chicago, LUMEN gross anatomy dissector: biceps brachii
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026: action listed as supinates forearm, flexes elbow, weakly flexes shoulder; musculocutaneous nerve. The page's own title and date were not shown.

sources.title: Loyola University Chicago, LUMEN gross anatomy dissector: triceps brachii
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026: long head from the infraglenoid tubercle; lateral head from the upper half of the posterior humerus; medial head deep on the lower half of the posterior humerus below the spiral groove; action: extends elbow, long head stabilises the shoulder joint, medial head retracts the capsule of the elbow joint on extension; inserts on the olecranon and posterior capsule; radial nerve.

sources.title: Loyola University Chicago, LUMEN gross anatomy dissector: coracobrachialis
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026: origin on the coracoid process with the short head of biceps; inserts on the upper half of the medial border of the humerus (other references give the middle third); action: flexes the arm and weakly adducts it; musculocutaneous nerve.

sources.title: TeachMeAnatomy: muscles of the arm
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026: the biceps brachii is the most superficial muscle of the anterior compartment, with a long head from the supraglenoid tubercle and a short head from the coracoid process; its function is supination of the forearm, and it also flexes the arm at the elbow and at the shoulder; coracobrachialis flexes the arm at the shoulder and weakly adducts it. An anatomy teaching site, not a university page. Its triceps section was not shown.

sources.title: TeachMeAnatomy encyclopaedia: brachialis
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026: in the anterior compartment, deep to the biceps brachii, forming the floor of the cubital fossa; flexes the elbow; musculocutaneous nerve with a contribution from the radial nerve.

sources.title: AnatomyZone: lateral head of triceps brachii
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026: the lateral and long heads lie superficially and the medial head deep to them; lateral head from the posterior humerus above the radial groove; the three heads converge on the olecranon; extends the forearm at the elbow; radial nerve.

sources.title: DocCheck Flexikon: triceps brachii muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026: the medial head is largely covered by the lateral and long heads, and only its distal part is visible from outside. An open medical encyclopedia edited by contributors; weaker than the preferred references and cited only beside them.

sources.title: Madsen, Marx, Millett, Rodeo, Sperling and Warren, Surgical anatomy of the triceps brachii tendon: anatomical study and clinical correlation (American Journal of Sports Medicine, 2006)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (abstract): dissection of eight cadaver elbows; the muscle of the medial head extended further distally than the long and lateral heads, and the medial head had a separate insertion deep to the common insertion of the other two, confluent at the olecranon. Volume 34, pages 1839 to 1843, as given in reference lists; the PubMed id is inferred from a Weill Cornell record (pubid16735585), not opened.

sources.title: Kholinne et al., The different role of each head of the triceps brachii muscle in elbow extension (Acta Orthopaedica et Traumatologica Turcica 52(3):201-205, 2018)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (abstract): ten healthy adults (8 men, 2 women) extended the elbow at 0, 45, 90, 135 and 180 degrees of shoulder elevation; surface EMG and movement data drove an OpenSim musculoskeletal model to estimate force. At 0 degrees the long head had significantly higher force and activation than the lateral and medial heads; at 90 degrees and above the medial head had significantly higher force than the other two. One summary mentioned a biomechanical simulator; a second found no cadaver component. DOI and PubMed id were not confirmed; co-author list not shown.

sources.title: Maeo, Wu, Huang, Sakurai, Kusagawa, Sugiyama, Kanehisa and Isaka, Triceps brachii hypertrophy is substantially greater after elbow extension training performed in the overhead versus neutral arm position (European Journal of Sport Science 23(7):1240-1250, 2023)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (abstract): 21 adults did cable elbow extensions with one arm overhead and the other in a neutral position, five sets of ten at seven tenths of the one-repetition maximum, twice a week for 12 weeks; MRI muscle volume. The overhead arm's volume gain was about 1.5-fold the neutral arm's for the long head and about 1.4-fold for the lateral and medial heads together and for the whole muscle. Training status of the participants was not confirmed by the excerpts.

sources.title: Stasinaki et al., Triceps Brachii Muscle Strength and Architectural Adaptations with Resistance Training Exercises at Short or Long Fascicle Length (Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology 3(2):28, 2018)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (abstract): nine novice women trained six weeks, one arm with cable push-downs and the other with overhead extensions, 6 sets of a 6-repetition maximum; strength and muscle thickness rose similarly in both arms and fascicle angle and length did not change. A commentary questioned the overhead loading; that is not a finding of the paper. Full author list not shown.

sources.title: Coratella et al., Biceps Brachii and Brachioradialis Excitation in Biceps Curl Exercise: Different Handgrips, Different Synergy (Sports 11(3):64, 2023)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (abstract): ten competitive bodybuilders did bilateral curls in six-repetition sets at an eight-repetition maximum with supinated, pronated and neutral grips; surface EMG. While lifting, the biceps and brachioradialis were more excited with the supinated grip than the other two, and the anterior deltoid less; while lowering, only the anterior deltoid differed. Full author list not shown.

sources.title: Levy et al., Function of the long head of the biceps at the shoulder: electromyographic analysis (2001)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (abstract): ten shoulders, dynamic EMG with wire electrodes, the elbow locked straight in a long arm brace with the forearm neutral; no electrical activity was found in the long head of the biceps during isolated shoulder motion. Journal and full author list were not confirmed (believed to be the Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery).

sources.title: Chalmers, Cip, Trombley, Cole, Wimmer, Romeo and Verma, Glenohumeral Function of the Long Head of the Biceps Muscle: An Electromyographic Analysis (Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine 2(2), 2014)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (abstract): 13 healthy volunteers, surface EMG of both biceps heads, deltoid, infraspinatus and brachioradialis during shoulder motion with and without elbow splinting and a 1-kg load; mean activity in both biceps heads was low; long-head activity rose significantly with flexion and abduction, short-head activity did not.

sources.title: Diplock, Hing and Marks, The long head of biceps at the shoulder: a scoping review (BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders, 2023)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (opening of the abstract): 214 articles in six themes; the biceps' role in glenohumeral elevation and stability in healthy shoulders is minimal, larger with rotator cuff failure or an absent tendon. Its exact wording on EMG was not seen; volume and article number not shown.

sources.title: Accessory heads of the biceps brachii muscle: a systematic review and meta-analysis (Journal of Anatomy, 2022)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (abstract, via a Czech research-output record): 78 articles, 10,603 upper limbs, random-effects meta-analysis; accessory heads in a minority of limbs, a single accessory head the commonest form; more often unilateral and in males, no significant side difference; falling prevalence over time; innervation and blood supply nearly identical to the main muscle and usually asymptomatic. Authors were not shown; the journal is inferred from the DOI prefix; the year from the record id. Population subgroup results were not seen.

singleSourceFunctionClaims: None among the six new function claims (each rests on three to five references).

The two shipped function claims the page reuses are single-source: forearm:biceps.function (A50) and forearm:brachialis.function (A51), as 03-anatomy-evidence.md §2 says. Corroborating references were found this time (see each shipped claim's upperArmUse); they are frozen claims, so adding sources is the database lane's call.
Non-function claims resting on one source: upper_arm.biceps.variation.1 (one meta-analysis) and upper_arm.triceps_long.selectivity.1 (one ten-person study).

Loyola LUMEN pages: page titles and dates not shown; the dissector text was quoted in the results.
disagreementsAndWording: Biceps at the shoulder: Kenhub and Loyola call it a weak flexor, TeachMeAnatomy lists shoulder flexion, Elsevier lists no shoulder action; EMG studies disagree (Levy: no long-head activity with the elbow braced; Chalmers: low activity rising with flexion and abduction) and a scoping review calls its part in raising the arm minimal in healthy shoulders. The function claim says 'weak help' and that one reference lists none; the selectivity claim states the EMG disagreement; no node action.
Biceps and forearm position: Coratella 2023 found more biceps activity palm up while lifting; Kleiber 2015 (A4) found no change. The selectivity claim states both.

Long head steadying the shoulder: StatPearls and IMAIOS say with the arm by the side (adducted); Radiopaedia says in abduction. The claim says it helps hold the head of the bone in its socket and names no arm position.

Long head shoulder adduction: Kenhub and IMAIOS list it; Radiopaedia lists extension only. The claim attributes both to 'references' and only extension becomes a node action (adduction is not an upper-arm region action).

Medial head at the surface: DocCheck says its lower part shows; Radiopaedia says largely deep; Madsen says its muscle reaches further toward the elbow; Kenhub says it cannot be felt. The appearance claim and a caveat say references differ.
Coracobrachialis adduction: Elsevier lists adduction first; Loyola and TeachMeAnatomy call it weak. The claim says 'helps draw it toward the body'.
Coracobrachialis insertion: Elsevier gives the middle third of the humerus, Loyola the upper half of its inner border. The claim says 'about halfway down'.

Brachialis edges: the shipped forearm claim says it 'may show at its sides'; this review confirmed only the outer edge (Kenhub video). The new upper-arm claim and the neutral shape note say outer edge; the shipped claim is frozen and stays on the forearm page.

Training studies on arm position (Maeo 2023: more volume gain overhead in every head; Stasinaki 2018: no difference) are stated together in a draft selectivity claim; the draft reason is the §1.2 / §8 policy conflict, not the evidence.
Akima et al. 2021 (PLOS One, PMC8174684): isometric surface EMG of the three heads; the abstract seen said activity mostly did not differ, but it was cut off mid-result, so it is not cited.
Triceps heads by force level (one older review: medial and lateral active from onset, long head at higher forces) was seen only second-hand and is not cited.
section12Checks: Layers: biceps surface, brachialis deep with a front outcrop, long and lateral heads surface, medial head deep with a back outcrop: supported (medial outcrop with a disagreement, above). Coracobrachialis deep: supported in part (felt in the armpit). No deviation.

Lateral and medial heads share every action: supported (both cross only the elbow and extend it). The medial head's pull on the elbow capsule is not a region action. Kholinne's modelled force difference by arm height is acute and does not change the actions; mappings stay 'shared'.
The biceps stays one node: supported. Its heads differ only at the shoulder (Chalmers: long-head activity rose with flexion and abduction, short head did not), where its role is weak.

Region actions: shoulder.flexion has a performer (coracobrachialis, prime); the biceps' part is left out. shoulder.extension: long head, assist. The long head and coracobrachialis also adduct the arm, which is not an upper-arm region action; adding shoulder.adduction is not proposed (the chest and back own it).
Brachioradialis as an external: supported by the rule (prime mover of elbow.flexion; curls load it).

Observation outside §1.2: the forearm's anconeus carries catalogMuscleKey 'triceps' (forearm nodes.ts), the upper arm's catalog key; region catalog keys are explicit (§1.1), so this may be harmless, but the registry lane should look.
policyQuestions: upper_arm.triceps_long.selectivity.2 is draft because §1.2 sends long-head regional-growth findings to selectivity claims while §8 says selectivity claims are never growth. The owner or the adversarial review decides.
